strengths: The paper identifies an interesting and plausible phenomenon—'Capability Degradation' when adapting generative MLLMs into discriminative single-embedding retrievers—and provides both qualitative and quantitative evidence (the F-solvable subset experiment) that is a reasonably creative way to isolate and measure the effect.

The proposed diagnose-generate-refine pipeline is a coherent, self-consistent framework: self-guided hard-negative mining, CoT-based minimal-edit triplet generation with VQA-based filtering, and grouped contrastive refinement with a dual loss (InfoNCE + in-group triplet margin) are all sensibly connected to the diagnosed problem.

Empirical results show consistent, non-trivial improvements over the Rbase starting point on both CIRR and FashionIQ, and the method attains state-of-the-art or near state-of-the-art numbers versus a reasonably broad set of recent baselines.

Ablations are fairly thorough: they isolate the contribution of self-guided mining vs random mining (with multiple seeds and variance reported), and progressively ablate CG, VC, and GR components, which supports the claimed contribution of each module.
A generalizability check across two backbones (Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B) suggests the method is not overfit to one specific foundation model.
Qualitative examples in Fig. 3 are illustrative and support the narrative of fine-grained grounding failure and recovery.
weaknesses: The core 'Capability Degradation' diagnostic in Fig. 1 is somewhat circular: the F-solvable subset is defined based on F's zero-shot VQA success, and then Rbase's R@1 is measured on this same subset via a very different (much harder, ranking over a full gallery) task; VQA match-or-not on a small candidate set is not directly comparable to top-1 ranking retrieval over a gallery, so the '62.33%' and '55.80%' numbers may partly reflect task-difficulty mismatch rather than pure capability loss due to adaptation. No control experiment (e.g., F evaluated as a retriever without fine-tuning, or Rbase evaluated via a VQA-style match protocol) is reported to isolate the adaptation effect from the task-format effect.

The generative calibration relies heavily on the foundation model F's own CoT and VQA judgments to both create and validate corrective triplets; since F is also the model whose reasoning is presumably degraded post-fine-tuning, there's a risk of confirmation bias/error propagation from F's imperfect judgments, and no human evaluation or error analysis of the generated triplet quality (e.g., accuracy of minimal edits, false-positive rate of VQA filtering) is provided.

No reported computational overhead, cost of the additional generation/mining stages, or statistics on how many corrective triplets are produced, filtered, and used, making it hard to assess practicality and reproducibility.

The main comparison tables lack error bars/multiple runs for the primary SOTA comparisons (only the random-mining ablation reports variance), so the significance of the reported gains (e.g., CIRR R@1 55.52 vs CIR-LVLM 53.64) is not statistically substantiated.

Some related methods (e.g., CIR-LVLM, TME, CCIN) are close in performance to ReCALL on several metrics (e.g., CIRR R@5, R@50; FashionIQ R@50), so the 'state-of-the-art' claim is only partial and should be tempered given the narrow margins on several metrics.

The paper's presentation has some redundancy/inconsistency (e.g., reference [42] and [43] appear to be duplicate entries for the same CIR-LVLM paper), and code is not yet released, which limits reproducibility verification at review time.

The hyperparameter choices (e.g., λ=0.30 vs 0.25, step counts) appear tuned per-dataset without an ablation showing sensitivity, raising questions about robustness of the method to hyperparameter selection.

The method's applicability is demonstrated only on two benchmarks (CIRR, FashionIQ); it is unclear how well the diagnose-generate-refine pipeline generalizes to other CIR datasets (e.g., CIRCO, GeneCIS) or to open-domain retrieval settings beyond fashion and NLVR2-derived data.

strengths: The paper addresses a conceptually interesting and underexplored issue in MLLM-based retrieval adaptation: the possible mismatch between a model's generative/step-wise reasoning capability and the discriminative single-embedding retrieval objective it is fine-tuned for.

The proposed diagnose-generate-refine pipeline is intuitive and modular, combining self-guided hard-instance mining, CoT-based corrective triplet synthesis, VQA-based filtering, and grouped contrastive refinement into a coherent framework.

Reasonably thorough ablation studies are provided (mining strategy, CG/VC/GR components, backbone generalization), and results on CIRR and FashionIQ show consistent, sometimes sizable, improvements over the authors' own baseline retriever.
The paper is clearly structured and the figures (especially Fig. 2) aid understanding of the overall pipeline.
weaknesses: The central claim of 'Capability Degradation' rests on a methodologically questionable analysis: the 'F-solvable subset' is defined precisely as examples where the foundation model F achieves 100% R@1 via VQA, so by construction this subset is biased toward F's strengths; the fact that a differently-optimized retriever (Rbase) scores lower on this cherry-picked subset does not unambiguously establish 'degradation' of reasoning ability versus simply reflecting different task formulations (generative multi-way VQA vs. single-vector retrieval against a large gallery, which is intrinsically harder). No control experiment (e.g., an Rbase-solvable subset tested on F) is shown to validate that this asymmetry is specifically a degradation phenomenon rather than an inherent capability/task mismatch.

The technical contribution, when stripped of the 'Capability Degradation' framing, largely reduces to a now-common recipe in CIR/retrieval literature: hard-negative mining from a trained retriever, LLM/VLM-based generation of corrective text for hard negatives, consistency filtering, and training with an auxiliary triplet/margin loss alongside InfoNCE. Several of these ideas (hard negative mining, self-training with LLM-generated hard triplets, grouped/triplet losses) already appear in prior CIR works (e.g., self-training boosted matching networks, CCIN, TME) cited by the paper, and the novelty claims are not clearly differentiated from this body of work beyond renaming it.

The 'Random Mining' ablation baseline is a weak strawman (uniformly sampling negatives from the top-50 candidate pool), which is not representative of stronger alternative mining strategies used elsewhere in the literature; this makes the claimed benefit of 'self-guided' mining less convincing as evidence of a fundamentally better approach rather than simply better negative selection.

No variance/significance reporting is provided for the main SOTA comparison tables (Tables 1 and 2), despite showing seed-averaged results in the ablation (Table 3); given that some improvements over competing SOTA methods are quite small (e.g., R@50 improvements of 0.36%–1.37%), the lack of statistical testing weakens the strength of the SOTA claims.

Reproducibility is limited: no code is released at submission time ('Code will be released soon'), the generation prompts for CoT-assisted synthesis and VQA-based filtering are not shown, and key details (number of synthesized triplets, filtering pass rates, cost/compute overhead of the generation pipeline) are omitted, making it difficult to assess the practicality and reproducibility of the method.

The claimed 'model-agnostic' generalization is tested only across two closely related backbones from the same model family (Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B); this is a narrow test of generalizability and does not substantiate claims of broad applicability across different MLLM architectures (e.g., LLaVA, InternVL).

Hyperparameters (learning rate, steps, loss weight λ) differ between CIRR and FashionIQ without clear justification or sensitivity analysis, raising concern about dataset-specific tuning that could inflate reported gains.

Qualitative evidence for the core phenomenon and the fix (Figs. 1 and 3) is based on a very small number of cherry-picked examples, which is insufficient to firmly establish the generality of the claimed degradation-and-recalibration effect beyond the quantitative subset analysis already critiqued above.

strengths: Identifies and clearly articulates an underexplored and practically relevant problem: 'Capability Degradation,' where adapting generative MLLMs into single-embedding discriminative retrievers causes a loss of fine-grained compositional reasoning present in the base model.

The diagnose-generate-refine pipeline is intuitive, model-agnostic, and well-motivated: mining hard failure cases from the retriever itself, using CoT-based generation from the foundation model to produce targeted corrective triplets, filtering with VQA-based consistency checks, and refining with a grouped contrastive objective that explicitly contrasts original and corrected triplets.

Strong and consistent empirical results: state-of-the-art performance on both CIRR and FashionIQ benchmarks, with clear and substantial relative gains over the Rbase starting point (e.g., +8.38% R@1 on CIRR, +7.16% average R@10 on FashionIQ).

Comprehensive ablation studies isolating the contribution of each pipeline component (self-guided vs. random mining, CoT generation, VQA quality control, grouped refinement), each showing incremental and sensible gains.

Generalizability experiment across a second, stronger foundation model (Qwen3-VL-8B) supports the claim that the framework is model-agnostic and that capability degradation is a persistent phenomenon rather than an artifact of a specific backbone.
Clear qualitative examples illustrating fine-grained failure modes (e.g., 'half sleeved,' 'facing the camera') and how ReCALL corrects them, reinforcing the quantitative claims.
weaknesses: The central quantitative evidence for 'Capability Degradation' (Fig. 1b) compares a discriminative embedding-similarity retriever against a generative VQA-based match/no-match judgment by F on an F-solvable subset. These are fundamentally different task formulations (independent single-embedding ranking over a large gallery vs. joint pairwise binary classification), so part of the observed gap may reflect this inherent asymmetry rather than purely a 'degradation' of internalized knowledge; this potential confound is not discussed or controlled for.

The generative calibration and quality-control stages both rely on the same foundation model F to produce and self-verify corrective triplets, raising concerns about confirmation bias/error propagation that are not empirically analyzed (e.g., no human-verified quality audit of generated triplets beyond the VQA self-check).

No statistical significance testing or repeated runs are reported for the main results tables (Tables 1 and 2) or the core ablation results in Table 4, only the random-mining baseline includes variance across seeds, making it harder to assess how much of the reported gains are robust versus run-to-run noise.

Reproducibility is currently limited: code is not yet released ('Code will be released soon'), and several important implementation details (e.g., exact prompt templates for CoT generation and VQA filtering, number of generated triplets per query, computational overhead of the generation pipeline) are not specified.

Evaluation is restricted to two standard CIR benchmarks (CIRR, FashionIQ); while these are the field's mainstream datasets, broader evaluation (e.g., additional domains or a stress test on more diverse compositional reasoning types) would strengthen claims of general applicability.
Hyperparameter choices (margin m, loss weight λ) are stated but not accompanied by sensitivity analysis, leaving it unclear how robust the method is to these settings.

Minor issues: duplicate reference entries for CIR-LVLM ([42] and [43]) point to the same paper; some figures (e.g., Fig. 4) lack precise numeric axis labeling in the text, requiring cross-referencing with the narrative for exact values.

strengths: Identifies and empirically documents an interesting and plausible phenomenon ('capability degradation') when adapting generative MLLMs into single-embedding discriminative retrievers, providing both qualitative examples and a quantitative gap measurement (Fig. 1) to motivate the work.

The diagnose-generate-refine pipeline is a coherent, well-engineered combination of self-guided hard-instance mining, CoT-based minimal-edit triplet synthesis, VQA-based filtering, and a grouped contrastive/triplet-margin refinement objective, each targeting a specific weakness of naive fine-tuning.

Extensive and informative ablations: comparison against random mining and hard-negative-without-edit baselines (with multiple random seeds and variance reported), component-wise ablation of CG/VC/GR, hyperparameter sensitivity grid (λ, margin), data-scale study, LoRA-rank/full fine-tuning ablation (showing degradation is not simply a capacity issue), and cross-backbone/cross-model transfer experiments (Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL, LLaVA-NeXT).

Consistent, non-trivial improvements over strong recent MLLM-based and dual-tower baselines on both CIRR and FashionIQ, including on the fine-grained Recall_subset metric designed to probe discriminative power.

Good reproducibility support: detailed prompts for retrieval encoding, VQA verification, and CoT generation are provided in the appendix, along with computational cost breakdowns and a human evaluation (92% accuracy) validating the reliability of the VQA-based filtering.

Candid failure-case analysis acknowledging false negatives, annotation sparsity, and residual spatial-reasoning limitations, which strengthens the credibility of the evaluation rather than overselling results.
weaknesses: The core motivating experiment (Fig. 1b) comparing Rbase's R@1 against F's 'VQA-based retrieval' on an 'F-solvable subset' is not fully specified: it is unclear whether F performs genuine full-gallery retrieval or simply reranks/verifies a candidate set (possibly derived from Rbase itself), which could bias the reported degradation gap; more methodological detail is needed to substantiate the claimed severity of degradation.

The VQA-Assisted Quality Control reuses the same foundation model F that generated the corrective edits, introducing a degree of self-referential/circular verification; the human-evaluation check (92% on 300 samples) partially mitigates but does not fully resolve this concern, and inter-annotator agreement is not reported.

Individual components (CoT self-correction, hard-negative mining, triplet margin loss, self-training/bootstrapping) are each well-established in prior LLM self-improvement and metric-learning literature; the contribution is primarily a task-specific integration rather than a fundamentally new technique.

Evaluation is limited to CIRR and FashionIQ; other common CIR benchmarks (e.g., CIRCO, GeneCIS, Fashion200k) are not included, limiting evidence of broader generalization across query/domain distributions.

The offline generation pipeline (Stages 2–3) requires substantial additional inference compute (10–14+ hours) using the foundation model over the training set, which, while framed as a one-time cost, adds non-trivial overhead and dependency on a capable foundation model that may not be available/reproducible in all settings.

Table 1/2 comparisons do not normalize for training cost or parameter budget relative to competing methods, making it harder to assess efficiency-adjusted gains against the strongest baselines (e.g., CIR-LVLM, TME).

strengths: The paper identifies and empirically motivates a plausible phenomenon ("capability degradation") when adapting generative MLLMs into discriminative retrievers, supported by both qualitative examples and a quantitative subset analysis (Fig. 1).

The diagnose-generate-refine pipeline is clearly described with well-organized stages (informative instance mining, CoT-based corrective triplet generation, VQA-based filtering, grouped contrastive refinement).

Extensive ablations are provided, including comparisons to random mining and hard-negative mining without textual correction (Tabs. 3, 7), LoRA rank/full fine-tuning control (Tab. 8), data-scale and hyperparameter sensitivity analyses, and cross-backbone generalization (Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL, LLaVA-NeXT).
Consistent and non-trivial improvements over the Rbase starting point on both CIRR and FashionIQ, with results that are competitive with or exceed several recent published baselines.
The supplementary material includes honest failure-case analysis (false negatives, ambiguous instructions, spatial-reasoning limits) and computational cost breakdowns, aiding transparency.
Small-scale human evaluation of the VQA filtering step (92% accuracy on 300 samples) provides some support for the reliability of the generated supervision.
weaknesses: The central 'capability degradation' evidence (Fig. 1b) compares Rbase's full-gallery retrieval performance on a subset selected precisely because the VQA-based foundation model succeeds there; this subset-selection process could inherently bias toward cases that favor pairwise verification over global embedding similarity, so the reported gap may partly reflect a difference between task formulations (one-vs-many binary matching vs. large-scale nearest-neighbor retrieval) rather than a clean measure of degraded reasoning.

The pipeline uses the same foundation model F both to generate corrective instructions and to verify them via VQA-based filtering, which risks self-consistency/circularity: F's own errors or biases can be reinforced rather than corrected, and no independent verifier or human-in-the-loop check is used at scale (only 300 samples audited post hoc).

A natural and much simpler baseline—using F directly as a VQA-based reranker on top of Rbase's retrieved candidates—is discussed conceptually (Fig. 1a) but never empirically compared against ReCALL, leaving open whether the complex diagnose-generate-refine pipeline is necessary versus a lightweight rerank step.

The core techniques (CoT-based data augmentation, hard-negative mining, VQA-based filtering, triplet/InfoNCE contrastive objectives) are individually well-established in the self-improvement/LLM and metric-learning literature; the contribution is primarily a combination/application to CIR rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Key hyperparameters (loss weight λ, margin m) are tuned separately per dataset (0.30/0.05 for FashionIQ vs. 0.25/0.05 for CIRR) via grid search on the validation set, raising some concern about benchmark-specific tuning rather than a truly model-agnostic default.
Evaluation is limited to two benchmarks (CIRR, FashionIQ); while standard in this subfield, this limits evidence for broader generalization claims implied by the 'model-agnostic framework' framing.

Some claims are stated with strong rhetorical certainty (e.g., 'unequivocal,' 'compellingly validates') that are not fully backed by statistical rigor (e.g., no variance/significance testing for the main results tables, only for the random-mining ablation).

strengths: Clearly motivated and empirically substantiated problem statement: the paper demonstrates 'capability degradation' both qualitatively (Fig. 1a) and quantitatively (Fig. 1b, F-solvable subset analysis), giving a concrete diagnostic basis for the proposed method rather than an assumed premise.

Comprehensive empirical validation: state-of-the-art results on both CIRR and FashionIQ, with consistent and substantial gains over the Rbase starting point (+8.38% R@1 on CIRR, +7.16% avg R@10 on FashionIQ).

Thorough and well-designed ablation suite covering each pipeline stage (mining strategy vs. random/hard-negative mining, CG/VC/GR component-wise contributions, hyperparameter sensitivity for the triplet loss, and data-scale trends), which convincingly isolates the contribution of each design choice.

Strong generalizability evidence: the framework is tested across different backbones (Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Qwen3-VL-8B, LLaVA-NeXT) and includes a cross-model data-transfer study, supporting the claimed model-agnostic nature of ReCALL.

Transparent reporting of computational costs, statistical robustness for the random-mining baseline (mean/std over 4 seeds), and human-verified reliability of the VQA-based filtering (92% accuracy on 300 samples), which strengthens reproducibility and trustworthiness of the reported numbers.

Candid failure-case analysis in the supplementary material (false negatives due to sparse annotations, ambiguous instructions, residual spatial reasoning limits) that acknowledges genuine limitations rather than overstating the method's capabilities.
weaknesses: The quantitative 'capability degradation' diagnosis (F-solvable subset via zero-shot VQA) compares two different task formulations (binary VQA matching vs. large-gallery ranking), which is not a fully controlled comparison and could partly reflect task-difficulty differences rather than purely a paradigm-conflict effect; a more controlled analysis (e.g., matched candidate pools) would strengthen the core motivating claim.

Potential circularity in using the same foundation model F both as the base retriever's initialization and as the generator/verifier of corrective supervision (CoT generation and VQA filtering); although the cross-model transfer experiment in the supplement partially addresses this, the self-referential diagnose-generate-refine loop could reinforce F's own blind spots rather than external knowledge.

Individual components (CoT-based instruction rewriting, hard-negative mining, triplet/contrastive losses) are largely adaptations of well-established techniques; the paper's novelty rests primarily on the specific combination and framing (diagnose-generate-refine) rather than on a fundamentally new technical mechanism.

Gains on broader-K metrics are comparatively modest (e.g., +0.36% R@50 on CIRR), suggesting the method's main benefit is concentrated in top-1/fine-grained discrimination rather than overall ranking quality.

Main result tables report single-run numbers without variance/error bars (only the random-mining ablation includes multiple seeds), making it harder to assess the statistical significance of the reported improvements over close competitors (e.g., CIR-LVLM, TME).

The offline generation cost (10–14+ hours per dataset) scales with dataset size and mining budget K, and while framed as a one-time cost, this could still be a practical bottleneck for scaling to substantially larger or continuously updated retrieval corpora, which is not discussed in depth.
